findings.issue_category: hard-coded cloud credentials in user data
findings.description: The user_data script exports a static AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in cleartext. EC2 user data is stored unencrypted and retrievable from the instance metadata service by any process on the host or via SSRF against the internet-facing web server, leaking long-lived IAM credentials.

Ingress allows TCP/22 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH on an instance that sits in a public subnet with a default route to an internet gateway, enabling brute-force and exploitation attempts against the management port.

The egress rule permits all protocols to 0.0.0.0/0, providing no outbound restriction and allowing a compromised host to exfiltrate data or reach command-and-control infrastructure. Ingress on port 80 is also open to the world with only cleartext HTTP configured and no TLS listener.
The EBS data volume does not set encrypted = true or a KMS key, so data written to the disk attached to the portal server is stored unencrypted.

The snapshot is derived from an unencrypted EBS volume and therefore inherits the lack of encryption at rest; snapshots are easily copied or shared across accounts, broadening exposure of the plaintext data.

No metadata_options block is defined, so the instance defaults to allowing token-less IMDSv1 requests. Combined with the hard-coded credentials in user data and the publicly reachable Apache server, an SSRF flaw would trivially expose instance metadata and user data.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the root EBS volume may be created unencrypted unless account-level EBS default encryption is enabled.

The instance is launched into a subnet with map_public_ip_on_launch = true whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway, placing it directly on the internet with no load balancer, NAT, or bastion boundary in front of it.
The VPC flow log destination bucket has no server-side encryption configuration, so sensitive network telemetry is stored without an explicitly enforced encryption policy or customer-managed key.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, ACL restriction, or bucket policy is defined for the flow log bucket, leaving protection of network metadata entirely dependent on account-level defaults and vulnerable to accidental public exposure.
The bucket has no policy denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false, permitting flow log data to be read or written over cleartext HTTP connections.

force_destroy = true on the flow-log archive bucket allows the bucket and all retained network logs to be deleted in a single operation, and no versioning or object lock protects the integrity of this security evidence.

map_public_ip_on_launch = true means every instance launched in this subnet automatically receives a public IP, and the associated route table routes 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway, so workloads are internet-reachable by default.

findings.issue_category: no private tier or default SG restriction
findings.description: Both subnets are attached to the single route table carrying a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway, so the VPC has no private tier and no segmentation between internet-facing and internal workloads. The implicitly created default security group is also left unmanaged (no aws_default_security_group block) and retains its permissive rules.
